titel: The basics of calls and puts
kurz: The two types of option, call and put, the four basic positions of buyer and option writer, and the unequal distribution of opportunity and risk between them.

bloecke.md:
An option is a contract about a right and, like every contract, has two sides. The buyer pays a premium and in return acquires the right to buy (**call**) or sell (**put**) a specified underlying at a price agreed in advance up to a specified date. The seller, the [[Option writer|option writer]], collects the premium and takes on the mirror-image obligation. They must deliver if the call buyer exercises and take delivery if the put buyer exercises. Once the contract has been concluded, they no longer have any choice.

In this respect the option differs from the share. A buyer of shares bears opportunity and risk symmetrically. When buying an option, the risk is limited to the premium paid, and the opportunity is preserved. The seller of an option has the reverse profile, with many small, certain gains and, rarely, a very large loss. Because both sides can be traded, the two contract types result in four basic positions. Every option strategy, even one with an exotic-sounding name, is a combination of these four positions, supplemented where applicable by the underlying itself.

bloecke.unter: The horizontal axis shows the side of the contract, the vertical axis the contract type; there are no other basic positions.

felder.text: Right to buy. Loss limited to the premium, gain open-ended. For prices that will soon rise significantly.
Obligation to deliver. Gain limited to the premium, loss theoretically unlimited if uncovered. For sideways to falling prices.
Right to sell. Loss limited to the premium, maximum gain at a price of zero. For sharply falling prices or hedging.
Obligation to take delivery. Gain limited to the premium, loss up to nearly the strike price. For sideways to rising prices.

bloecke.md:
## Content of the option contract

An option is fully described by six details. Without all six, you do not know your own position.

- The **underlying** can be a share, an index, a currency pair or a commodity future. With index options, there is nothing to deliver; they are cash-settled.
- The **[[Strike price|strike price]]** (strike, K) is the price at which the underlying may be bought or sold. It is fixed and does not change during the term. Regular dividends do not lead to any adjustment for Eurex equity options, but extraordinary corporate actions do.
- The **expiry date** is the last day on which the right exists. On Eurex, for standard maturities, this is the third Friday of the expiry month.
- The **[[Contract size|contract size]]** states how many units of the underlying a contract covers. For equity options, 100 shares is usual. For index options, it is replaced by a multiplier in euros per index point; for the EURO STOXX 50 option OESX, this is €10 per point according to the Eurex product specification. The smallest price change of 0.1 points corresponds to €1 there.
- The **exercise style** is American (at any time) or European (only on the expiry date).
- **Settlement** takes place by physical delivery of the underlying or by cash settlement of the difference.

The premium is always quoted per unit of the underlying, but it is paid for the whole contract. This is where confusion most often arises.

An equity option with a premium of €2.50 costs €250 with 100 shares per contract, and not €2.50. Conversely, the value of the position changes by up to €100 when the price of the underlying changes by one euro. The change reaches the full amount only for an option that is in the money on the expiry date, and approximately for an option that is deep in the money. Investors who plan position sizes on the basis of the displayed premium are out by a factor equal to the contract size. With short positions, the risk is in any case measured by the notional value of the contract and not by the premium.

bloecke.formel:
Long call:  P/L = max(S_T - K, 0) - P
Short call: P/L = P - max(S_T - K, 0)
Long put:   P/L = max(K - S_T, 0) - P
Short put:  P/L = P - max(K - S_T, 0)
bloecke.erklaerung: max(x, 0) stands for the larger of the two values x and zero. An option never has a negative value for the buyer, because in that case they let it expire. That is why their loss is limited to the premium. The buyer's and the seller's lines add up to zero at every closing price. Before fees, an option therefore only redistributes money between the two sides.
variablen: price of the underlying on the expiry date
premium per unit of the underlying
profit or loss per unit, excluding fees and taxes
bloecke.beispiel: K = 100, P = 5, S_T = 112: long call = max(12, 0) - 5 = +7 per share. Short call = 5 - 12 = -7 per share.

bloecke.md:
The two break-even points are 105 and 95. A call only pays off above the strike price plus premium, a put only below the strike price minus premium. The underlying therefore has to move in the right direction, far enough and in time. With options, it is normal for the buyer to judge the direction correctly and still lose money.

The premium itself is made up of intrinsic value and time value. How it is split and why the time value inevitably falls to zero is covered in the next lesson.

bloecke.unter: The line bends at the strike price and crosses the zero line at 105; below the strike price, the buyer always loses the full premium.

bloecke.md:
A share is trading at €100. In variant A, an investor buys 100 shares and invests €10,000. In variant B, they buy a call contract on 100 shares with a strike price of 100, a term of three months and a premium of €5 per share; their outlay is €500.

- If the share is at 112 on the expiry date, variant A gains €1,200, that is, 12% on the outlay. Variant B gains (12 - 5) × 100 = €700, that is, 140% on the outlay.
- If the share is unchanged at 100, variant A neither gains nor loses. Variant B loses the full €500, that is, 100%.
- If the share is at 80, variant A loses €2,000 and still holds 100 shares. Variant B loses €500 and no longer holds anything.

The leverage comes from the contract size combined with a small outlay; no borrowed money is needed for it. The drawback is that an unchanged price of the underlying means a total loss for the option buyer.

bloecke.titel: Profit and loss on the expiry date for the share and a long call
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation per share. The call limits the loss to €5, but in return misses out on the first €5 of price gain.

bloecke.md:
## The option writer's position

Writing an option, that is, selling it, is similar to selling insurance. The option writer is certain to receive the premium, whereas their risk is open. With an uncovered short call, the loss has no upper limit. If the underlying rises from 100 to 180, the option writer has to buy at 180 and deliver at 100. After deducting the premium, they lose €75 per share or €7,500 per contract. With a short put, the loss is mathematically limited, but only because a price cannot fall below zero. The maximum loss is the strike price minus the premium, here €95 per share or €9,500 per contract.

Covered variants such as the covered call and the cash-secured put change this risk profile and are the subject of a separate lesson. The uncovered position is, however, a better starting point, because it shows what the option writer has sold.

bloecke.titel: Short put with strike price 100 and premium received of 5
bloecke.unter: Above the strike price, the result is a constant plus 5; below it, the result falls steadily, to minus 35 at a price of 60 and only to minus 95 at a price of zero.

bloecke.titel: Result per contract on 100 shares in euros (strike price 100, premium 5 per share)

bloecke.md: In every row, the call buyer and the call writer cancel each other out, as do the put buyer and the put writer. An options market does not create value; it transfers risk in exchange for money. With this knowledge, you can see through presentations in which an option strategy generates income without anything in return. What appears in one place as premium income is, somewhere else, the price of a hedge that someone has bought.

## American and European options

A **European** option can only be exercised on the expiry date, an **American** one at any time during its term. The names have nothing to do with the trading venue. On Eurex, the rule of thumb is that index options such as ODAX on the DAX and OESX on the EURO STOXX 50 are European and cash-settled. Equity options there are usually American with physical delivery. Writers of equity options must therefore read the contract specification before their first trade, because the exercise style determines the risk of early [[Assignment|assignment]].

For the buyer, the American variant is an advantage, but one that rarely matters in practice. With early exercise, they give up the remaining time value of the option, and a sale almost always brings in more than exercise. For the option writer, on the other hand, exercise is a practical problem, because it is not announced to them in advance.

An American call on a share that pays no dividend is never exercised before the expiry date if the holder acts rationally, because a sale always brings in at least as much. This changes when a dividend is due. A call that is deep in the money has hardly any time value left, and the buyer receives the distribution if they exercise before the ex-dividend date. The writer of such a call then finds a short share position or a delivery obligation in their securities account the next morning. With American puts, early exercise can make sense as soon as the price is very low and the interest rate is significant.

## The warrant and its ratio

The contracts described so far are exchange-traded standard options with a clearing house as counterparty. The warrant, which private investors in Germany come across far more often, is legally a bearer bond (Inhaberschuldverschreibung) issued by a bank. The issuer sets the price itself, investors cannot become option writers, and if the issuer becomes insolvent, the investor is an unsecured insolvency creditor who faces a partial or total loss regardless of the underlying.

Technically, the warrant differs in having a **[[Subscription ratio|ratio]]**. It states how many units of the underlying a single warrant relates to. At 0.1, you need ten warrants for one share; at 0.01, a hundred warrants for a claim to one index point. An index warrant with a strike price of 23,000 and a ratio of 0.01 has an intrinsic value of 1,000 × 0.01 = €10 at an index level of 24,000. An overlooked ratio therefore leads to calculation errors by a factor of 10 or 100.

The following rules apply to private investors in Germany. Premiums collected by the option writer are capital income under Section 20(1) no. 11 EStG (Income Tax Act). If they later pay for a closing transaction, this amount is set off as negative income. Gains from cash settlement are income from derivative transactions (Termingeschäfte) under Section 20(2) sentence 1 no. 3 EStG; the calculation of the gain is governed by Section 20(4) sentence 5 EStG. The Annual Tax Act 2024 (Jahressteuergesetz) abolished without replacement the former loss offsetting limit of €20,000 a year for derivative transactions. Losses go into the general loss pot and, under Section 20(6) EStG, may not be offset against employment income or other types of income. Legal position as of September 2026; not tax advice.
The buyer knows their maximum loss on the day of purchase, the option writer their maximum gain on the day of sale. Both figures are already in the contract; everything else depends on the price.

mitnehmen: An option distributes rights and obligations unequally, because the buyer pays the premium and has a right, while the option writer receives it and has an obligation.
The four basic positions are sufficient because every strategy can be built from them, supplemented where applicable by the underlying.
The break-even point is the strike price plus premium for a call and the strike price minus premium for a put, so the right direction alone is not enough.
Contract size and ratio determine the size of the position; the displayed premium is never the full amount.
American options can be exercised at any time; on Eurex, equity options are usually American with delivery and index options European with cash settlement.

begriffe.text: The seller of an option. They collect the premium and take on the obligation to deliver (call) or take delivery (put) on exercise. Only the other side has a choice.
The price set in the option contract at which the underlying may be bought or sold, also called the strike or exercise price. It remains constant over the term.
Number of units of the underlying per option contract, usually 100 shares for equity options. For index options, a multiplier in euros per index point replaces the number of units.
For warrants and certificates, states how many units of the underlying a single security relates to. At 0.01, one warrant corresponds to one hundredth of the underlying.
The exercise of an option by the other side, seen from the option writer's point of view. With American options, it is possible at any time and is not announced in advance.
